issues.legal_issue: A law creating a state monopoly is protected against a challenge based on the right to carry on a trade, while incidental effects on other fundamental rights do not invalidate the monopoly provision.
material_facts: The challenged law restricted the purchase and transport of the commodity to the State, its authorised officers, or agents for the relevant area.
The law was intended to create a state monopoly in the trade.
The challenge relied on fundamental rights concerning property and the carrying on of trade.
issues.conclusion: The creation of a state monopoly is permitted by the latter part of Article 19(6), and the monopoly provision cannot be invalidated under the right to carry on a trade merely because it restricts citizens from that trade. An indirect or incidental effect on another fundamental right does not invalidate the monopoly provision, although provisions that are not essential to the monopoly must be assessed separately.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(6)(ii), as amended, permits laws relating to the State carrying on a trade, business, industry or service to the complete or partial exclusion of citizens; such a monopoly is presumed reasonable and in the interests of the general public for purposes of Article 19(1)(g). Only provisions integral and essential to creating the monopoly receive that protection. Other provisions must satisfy the ordinary constitutional tests, and a direct effect on another right under Article 19(1) must be assessed under the corresponding clause. The Court relied on the direct-versus-indirect-effect approach in A. K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, Ram Singh v. State of Delhi, Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India and State of Bombay v. R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala; it also referred to Saghir Ahmed v. State of U.P., Parbhani Transport Co-operative Society Ltd. v. Regional Transport Authority, Dosa Satyanarayanamurty v. Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation and H. C. Narayanappa v. State of Mysore on state monopolies.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_monopo: A person challenged the constitutionality of a law creating a state monopoly.
predicates.state_is_the_monopolist: The law provides for the State itself to carry on the monopolised trade or business.
predicates.challenged_provision_is_integral_to_crea: The challenged provision is essential to creating the state monopoly, rather than merely incidental to its operation.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an essential provision of a law under which the State carries on a monopoly, that provision is valid against a challenge based on the right to carry on a trade.

issues.legal_issue: An incidental price-control provision in a state-monopoly law is valid when its restrictions are reasonable and in the interests of the general public.
material_facts: The law required the State Government to fix the purchase price after consulting an advisory committee.
The price-fixing provision was not essential to the operation of the monopoly.
The price was fixed in consultation with the committee, and the petitioner neither established that it was unfair nor produced evidence that it was unreasonable.
The material before the Court indicated that the price compared favourably with prices in previous years and was intended to provide growers a fair return.
issues.conclusion: The price-fixing restrictions were reasonable and in the interests of the general public, and the provision was valid.
issues.legal_principle: A provision that is not essential or integral to creating a state monopoly is not protected merely by Article 19(6)(ii); its validity must be tested under the first part of Article 19(6) as to the right to carry on a trade and under Article 19(5) as to the right to property. The Court held that the price-fixing restriction satisfied those tests because it was intended to protect growers from hardship and there was no showing that the price was unfair or unreasonable. The constitutional framework applied was Articles 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), 19(5) and 19(6).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_incidental_price_control and price_control_not_essential_to_monopoly and price_fixed_after_advisory_consultation and price_not_shown_unfair_or_unreasonable

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_incidental_p: A person challenged a price-control provision included in a law creating a state monopoly.
predicates.price_control_not_essential_to_monopoly: The price-control provision is incidental rather than essential to creating the monopoly.
predicates.price_fixed_after_advisory_consultation: The State fixed the price after consulting an advisory body.
predicates.price_not_shown_unfair_or_unreasonable: The challenger did not establish that the fixed price was unfair or unreasonable.

issues.definition: An incidental price-control provision is valid when the State fixes the price after advisory consultation and the challenger does not establish that it is unfair or unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: The State may use agents to operate a state monopoly if they conduct the trade strictly on the State's behalf and for its benefit.
material_facts: The law authorised the Government, authorised government officers, and agents for the relevant areas to purchase or transport the commodity.
The Court construed the officers and agents contemplated by the law as acting for the Government and for its benefit.
The Court accepted that using agents could be appropriate where operating the trade through government departments or employees would be inexpedient.
issues.conclusion: The statutory authorisation for government officers and agents to operate the monopoly was valid, provided the agents act strictly on behalf of the State and not for themselves.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(6)(ii) permits the State to conduct a monopoly through its departments, officers, or agents, but any agent must act for the State and its benefit, within the strict and narrow sense of agency. Whether an arrangement is genuine agency depends on its substance, including the agreement and the circumstances in which it was made. The Court upheld the relevant statutory provisions on the construction that they contemplated only agency consistent with those limits.

predicates.state_monopoly_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the operation of a trade that the State has made a monopoly.
predicates.state_trade_requires_operational_assista: The State's operation of the trade requires assistance from officers or other persons.
predicates.proposed_agents_act_strictly_for_state: The persons assisting the State conduct the trade on its behalf and for its benefit, rather than for themselves.

issues.definition: When operating a state monopoly requires assistance, the State may use persons who conduct the trade strictly on its behalf and for its benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A rule governing state-monopoly agency appointments is invalid if it leaves the terms of the agency agreement to an officer's discretion instead of prescribing them by rules.
material_facts: The rule required an appointed agent to execute an agreement in whatever form the Government directed.
The rules prescribed an application form but did not prescribe the form or principal terms of the agency agreement.
The rule therefore left the terms to be set on an ad hoc basis by the officer concerned.
issues.conclusion: The rule was invalid because the terms and conditions of the agency agreement had to be prescribed by rules and could not be left to an officer's discretion.
issues.legal_principle: Under the rule-making authority in section 18, the principal terms and conditions of an agency used to operate the monopoly must be prescribed by rules. Leaving those terms to the ad hoc choice of an officer exceeds the State Government's competence. The Court accordingly held Rule 7(5) invalid.

predicates.state_monopoly_agent_appointment_proceed: The proceeding concerns a rule for appointing agents to operate a state monopoly.
predicates.agreement_terms_left_to_officer_discreti: The rule leaves the terms of the agent's agreement to the discretion of a government officer.
predicates.principal_terms_not_prescribed_by_rules: The rules do not prescribe the principal terms and conditions of the agency agreement.

issues.definition: A rule for appointing state-monopoly agents is invalid when it leaves the agreement terms to an officer and the rules do not prescribe the principal terms.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement does not establish the strict agency required for a state monopoly when the purported agent carries on the trade on personal account and the State is not accountable for the agent's acts.
material_facts: The agreement required the purported agent to finance the transactions involved in purchasing, collecting, storing, processing, transporting and disposing of the commodity.
The agreement left the purported agent with profits after the specified payments and made the agent bear losses in specified circumstances.
The purported agent was not made accountable to the State, and the State was not responsible for the agent's actions.
The agreement was made under a rule that did not prescribe the principal terms of the agency.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was invalid because it did not make the purported agent a strict and narrow agent of the State; the State could not implement the law through agents appointed under that agreement.
issues.legal_principle: For a state monopoly to be carried on through agents under Article 19(6)(ii), the agents must act at every stage on behalf of the State and for its benefit, rather than conduct the trade partly for their own benefit. Personal interests in profits or losses, lack of accountability to the State, and the State's lack of responsibility for the agent's actions are inconsistent with that relationship. The Court applied section 3(1)(c) and Article 19(6)(ii), distinguishing strict agency in this constitutional setting from the broader commercial meaning of agency discussed in Ex parte Bright in re Smith and Weiner v. Harris.

rule.if: challenge_to_state_monopoly_agent_agreement and purported_agent_carries_on_trade_for_own_account and purported_agent_bears_business_profit_or_loss and purported_agent_not_accountable_to_state and state_not_responsible_for_agent_actions

predicates.challenge_to_state_monopoly_agent_agreem: The proceeding challenges an agreement used to appoint persons to operate a state monopoly.
predicates.purported_agent_carries_on_trade_for_own: The purported agent conducts the trade at least partly on the agent's own account rather than solely on behalf of the State.
predicates.purported_agent_bears_business_profit_or: The agreement gives the purported agent a personal interest in business profits or makes the agent personally bear business losses.
predicates.purported_agent_not_accountable_to_state: The purported agent is not accountable to the State for the conduct of the trade.
predicates.state_not_responsible_for_agent_actions: The State is not responsible for the purported agent's actions.

issues.definition: An agreement is invalid, and cannot be used by the State to operate its monopoly, when the purported agent conducts the trade for personal account, bears business profits or losses, is not accountable to the State, and the State is not responsible for the agent's actions.
